topic.name: Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes of Rational Functions

question.text: Find the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{2x+5}{2x^3+2x+6}.$
question.explanation:
The horizontal asymptote is $y=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^3.$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x)&=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{2x+5}{2x^3+2x+6}\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{\Bigl(\dfrac{2x}{x^3}+\dfrac{5}{x^3}\Bigr)}{\Bigl(\dfrac{2x^3}{x^3}+\dfrac{2x}{x^3}+\dfrac{6}{x^3}\Bigr)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{\Bigl(\dfrac{2}{x^2}+\dfrac{5}{x^3}\Bigr)}{\Bigl(2+\dfrac{2}{x^2}+\dfrac{6}{x^3}\Bigr)}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{0+0}{2+0+0}\\[5pt] &=0. \end{align*}

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ is $y=0.$

example.title: Identifying the Horizontal Asymptote of a Rational Function

question.text: Given that the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{5x^2-6}{cx^2+32x+8}$ is $y=\dfrac{1}{4},$ find the value of $c.$
question.explanation:
The horizontal asymptote is $y=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^2.$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x)&=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{5x^2-6}{cx^2+32x+8}\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{\Bigl(\dfrac{5x^2}{x^2}-\dfrac{6}{x^2}\Bigr)}{\Bigl(\dfrac{cx^2}{x^2}+\dfrac{32x}{x^2}+\dfrac{8}{x^2}\Bigr)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{\Bigl(5-\dfrac{6}{x^2}\Bigr)}{\Bigl(c+\dfrac{32}{x}+\dfrac{8}{x^2}\Bigr)}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5-0}{c+0+0}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{c}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \begin{align*} \dfrac{5}{c}&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\[5pt] c&=20. \end{align*}

example.title: Identifying the Horizontal Asymptote of a Rational Function

question.explanation:
The horizontal asymptote is $y=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^5.$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x)&=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{11x^5-9x^6}{2x^5-1}\\[5pt] &\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{11x^5}{x^5}-\dfrac{9x^6}{x^5}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2x^5}{x^5}-\dfrac{1}{x^5}\right)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{\left(11 - 9x \right)}{\left(2-\dfrac{1}{x^5}\right)}\\[5pt] &=\lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{11-9x}{2-0}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2} \lim_\limits{x \rightarrow \infty} (11-9x)\\[5pt] &=-\infty. \end{align*}

The limit does not come out to a finite number. Therefore, there is no horizontal asymptote.

example.title: Identifying When a Rational Function has No Horizontal Asymptote

question.explanation:
First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^5.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

\begin{align*} \lim_{x\to\infty} \,\,\dfrac {8x^6 + 5}{2x^5 - 7x} &= \lim_{x\to\infty} \,\,\dfrac {\Bigl(\dfrac {8x^6}{x^5} + \dfrac {5}{x^5} \Bigr)}{\Bigl(\dfrac {2x^5}{x^5} - \dfrac {7x}{x^5} \Bigr)}\\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to\infty} \,\,\dfrac {\Bigl(8x + \dfrac {5}{x^5}\Bigr)}{\Bigl(2 - \dfrac {7}{x^4} \Bigr)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8x + 0}{2 - 0} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{x\to\infty} \,\, 4x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\infty}. \end{align*}
